bibliographic.title: Large language models improve clinical decision making of medical students through patient simulation and structured feedback: a randomized controlled trial
bibliographic.authors: Emilia Brügge, Sarah Ricchizzi, Malin Arenbeck, Marius Niklas Keller, Lina Schur, Walter Stummer, Markus Holling, Max Hao Lu, Dogus Darici
bibliographic.citation_apa: Brügge, E., Ricchizzi, S., Arenbeck, M., Keller, M. N., Schur, L., Stummer, W., Holling, M., Lu, M. H., & Darici, D. (2024). Large language models improve clinical decision making of medical students through patient simulation and structured feedback: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education, 24, 1391. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06399-7

methodology.study_design: double-blind two-group randomized controlled trial with repeated measures ANOVA
methodology.sample_description: medical students at the University of Münster, Germany during winter term 2023/2024
methodology.technology_context: LLM prompts to simulate patients with different symptoms in medical history conversations; ChatGPT Playground interface; AI-generated structured feedback after simulated conversations

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study evaluates educational outcomes of LLM-based patient simulation and feedback for medical students; the provided text does not address conversational AI governance, accountability, guardrails, audit, compliance, observability, or human oversight mechanisms.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the article uses LLMs for realistic medical history conversations in a regulated healthcare education context, its primary contribution is an RCT on clinical decision-making training effectiveness rather than governance of conversational LLM systems. No governance, risk control, audit, or supervisory framework is examined in the supplied excerpts.

appraisal.notes: Clear RCT objective and analysis with inter-rater reliability reported (ICC = 0.924), but very small sample (n=21) and reliance on ChatGPT Playground limits generalizability and reproducibility; ethics/reflexivity not substantively addressed in provided text.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are internally coherent for an educational efficacy question, but sample adequacy is limited and the supplied text offers little relevance to conversational governance mechanisms in regulated LLM deployments.

coding.theme: LLM-supported clinical training through simulated conversations
coding.subtheme: structured feedback after AI patient interactions

synthesis.main_claim: LLM-simulated medical history conversations combined with structured AI feedback improved medical students' clinical decision-making scores more than simulation alone after four training sessions.
synthesis.contribution: Provides empirical RCT evidence that LLM-based patient simulation with automated feedback can support CDM training in medical education as a cost-effective supplement.
synthesis.limitations: Small sample (n=21); used ChatGPT Playground/ChatGPT 3.5 with training data through January 2022; ongoing model updates may affect reproducibility; governance implications not analyzed.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude as central or supporting governance evidence; may serve only as peripheral contextual background on LLM conversational use in regulated medical education if a broader scoping note is needed.

evidence.claim: Study uses LLMs to simulate patient-doctor medical history conversations and provide structured feedback
evidence.excerpt: we explored the potential of using Large Language Models (LLM) to simulate patient-doctor interactions and provide structured feedback

evidence.claim: RCT design with control and feedback groups
evidence.excerpt: In our double-blind randomized design, the control group participated in simulated medical history conversations with AI patients (control group), while the intervention group, in addition to simulated conversations, also received AI-generated feedback on their performances (feedback group)
Our final sample included 21 medical students (agemean = 22.10 years, semestermean = 4, 14 females)

evidence.claim: Feedback group outperformed control on CDM after four sessions
evidence.excerpt: After only four training sessions, the feedback group (3.60 ± 0.13) outperformed the control group (3.02 ± 0.12), F (1,18) = 4.44, p = .049 with a strong effect size, partial η2 = 0.198

evidence.claim: Specific LLM technology context includes ChatGPT
evidence.excerpt: One emerging technology with the potential to make CDM even more accessible is the use of LLMs, such as ChatGPT

evidence.claim: Study conducted as two-group randomized-controlled study at University of Münster
evidence.excerpt: We conducted a two-group randomized-controlled study during winter term 2023/2024 at the University of Münster, Germany and used the large language model

evidence.claim: No prior LLM patient-simulation studies implemented feedback at time of reporting
evidence.excerpt: Among the few studies that exist on LLM-generated patient simulations [21–24], none have implemented feedback or debriefing at the time of reporting

evidence.claim: Authors note opportunities and challenges of LLM patient simulations but governance is not specified
evidence.excerpt: Additionally, we outlined the opportunities and challenges associated with using LLM for patient simulations

evidence.claim: Reproducibility limitation due to evolving language model
evidence.excerpt: A more significant limitation is the ongoing development of the language model, which may affect reproducibility

evidence.claim: ChatGPT Playground interface used for execution
evidence.excerpt: the study used the “Playground” interface of ChatGPT for its execution
